sentences.text: Citipati was among the largest members of the oviraptorid family, reaching lengths between 2.5 and 2.9 meters and weighing from 75 to 110 kilograms.
This dinosaur possessed a short, highly pneumatized skull that ended in a stout, toothless beak made of horn.
Unlike most theropods, Citipati featured an unusually long neck paired with a significantly shortened tail.
Citipati laid the largest known definitive oviraptorid eggs, which measure 18 centimeters in length.
Remarkably, a specific individual survived a healed injury to its ulna bone while still incubating its nest.
The famous specimen nicknamed 'Big Momma' was found sitting on a clutch of eggs in a nesting position.
Remains of this animal were first collected in the 1990s at the Ukhaa Tolgod locality within the Djadochta Formation.
A small fossilized oviraptorid embryo, cataloged as specimen IGM 100/971, was discovered in 1993 during an expedition in the Gobi Desert.
In 2001, James M. Clark, Mark A. Norell, and Rinchen Barsbold formally named the genus Citipati and the species C. osmolskae based on holotype IGM 100/978.
Specimen IGM 100/1004, which was found in 1995, was not officially assigned to Citipati osmolskae until 2018.
Analysis of the brooding posture indicates that Citipati had long pennaceous feathers and a complete feather covering on its body.
Long feathers extending onto the arms and tail likely served to protect eggs and young from environmental elements.
Fossils show nesting specimens sitting atop egg clutches with limbs spread symmetrically and front limbs covering the nest perimeter.
Citipati likely fed on tougher vegetation than other herbivorous theropods in its environment, with a bite force estimated between 349.3 N and 499.0 N.
Juvenile troodontid remains found near a nest suggest that adults may have brought prey to feed their young, hinting at an omnivorous diet.
In 2020, Gregory F. Funston and colleagues established the new subfamily Citipatiinae to separate Citipati from Oviraptor.
Citipati lived in Asia during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 75 to 71 million years ago.
The dinosaur inhabited arid to semiarid environments consisting of large sand dunes and short-lived water bodies.
Researchers debate whether remains from the nearby Zamyn Khondt locality represent a second species of Citipati.
It is also debated whether juvenile troodontid skulls found near Citipati nests were prey, nest raiders, or evidence of nest parasitism.
Some experts question whether a specific IGN specimen represents a second species of Citipati or a completely distinct genus.
